Frankenstein Authorship Myth. A widespread misconception holds that Frankenstein refers to the monster itself, when in fact Frankenstein is the name of the scientist, Victor Frankenstein, and the creature he creates is the monster or remains nameless. This confusion persists because the creature has become iconic while its creator's name has faded from popular memory.

Victor Frankenstein is the scientist, not the monster. The novel is his story, told in first person through letters and narrative. The creature itself is never given a name in the novel. It is referred to only as "the creature," "the monster," or "the being"—calling it "Frankenstein" fundamentally misidentifies the work's protagonist.

Mary Shelley published the novel in 1818 when she was just twenty years old, with no author attribution on the first edition. The creature is intelligent and articulate in the novel, capable of speech and philosophical reflection, far different from the inarticulate brute of popular culture and stage adaptations.

The Gothic tradition of the 1800s often adapted stories loosely for dramatic effect. Stage versions beginning with Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus in 1823 shifted focus to the monster, reinforcing the name confusion. The creature's anguish stems from abandonment and rejection by his creator and society, making him tragic rather than purely evil.
